title: Repair — The Physical Language of Apology
hook: An apology is judged by the body saying it, and many men get the words right while their posture, voice and timing say they do not mean them.
why:
Most people can tell a real apology from a performance within a second or two, and they rarely judge by the words alone. “I'm sorry” said with folded arms, a lifted chin and a glance at the clock is not an apology; it is a request for the subject to be closed. The same words said quietly, face to face, after listening, with a body that is not defending itself, can begin to mend something that seemed broken.

Many men find apology hard. Some were taught that it is weakness; some simply do not notice that one is owed. This chapter covers what research says makes an apology work; the evidence that men set a higher bar for what needs an apology; why timing matters, and why too early can be as bad as too late; what an apology looks like in the body; why a little visible embarrassment helps; the difference between guilt, which repairs, and shame, which hides; and what to do after the apology, when the other person is not yet ready to forgive. It follows the repair attempts of the previous chapter to their conclusion.

teach.p:
In 2016 Roy Lewicki, Beth Polin and Robert Lount tested which parts of an apology matter. They identified six common components: an expression of regret, an explanation of what went wrong, an acknowledgement of responsibility, a declaration of repentance, an offer of repair and a request for forgiveness. Then they asked hundreds of people to rate apologies containing different combinations.

Apologies with more components were rated as more effective. But two components mattered far more than the rest. The most important by a wide margin was acknowledging responsibility: saying plainly that you did it and that it was your fault, without excuses. The second was an offer of repair: saying what you will do to put it right. The least important was asking for forgiveness.

The study used written apologies, so it says nothing directly about tone, posture or timing, and the researchers noted that. But it gives the words a shape. A good apology says what you did, that it was on you, that you regret it, and what you will do now. It does not hide behind an explanation, and it does not make the other person's forgiveness the point.

The rest of this chapter is about the body that delivers those words. The figures here show the moment before: one man with a hand on his chest, head slightly lowered, facing a man whose arms are still folded. The words he is about to say matter. So does everything else about how he is standing.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if apologies that acknowledged responsibility and offered repair were rated no better than those that did not. Lewicki and colleagues found that they were rated much better, though in written scenarios, so real apologies may depend more on delivery than their study could show.

teach.p:
It is often said that women apologise more than men. In 2010 Karina Schumann and Michael Ross asked why. In a diary study, men and women recorded the offences they committed and the apologies they made each day. Women did report more apologies, but they also reported committing more offences. When either sex felt they had done something wrong, they apologised at about the same rate, roughly four times out of five.

In a second study, men rated the same imagined and remembered offences as less severe than women did, and those severity ratings predicted whether an apology seemed to be owed. The difference, Schumann and Ross concluded, was not that men refused to apologise but that they had a higher threshold for noticing that they had caused offence.

That has a practical consequence. If you are a man, you are more likely than the person you hurt to think that what happened was minor. So you need to read the other person rather than your own judgment of the offence. The signs are often physical and indirect: a cooler greeting, as the chapter on greetings described; short answers; a silence where there used to be talk; a friend who stops turning up; arms that stay folded around you; a body turned slightly away.

The figures here stand turned away from each other. If a relationship has started to look like this and you do not know why, the first question is whether you did something that you have rated as minor and they have not.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men apologised less even when they agreed they had caused offence. Schumann and Ross found they did not, though their samples were Canadian students, and thresholds may differ in other groups.

teach.p:
It seems obvious that a quicker apology is better. In 2005 Cynthia Frantz and Courtney Bennigson found that it is not always so. In small studies of real and imagined conflicts, apologies that came later in a conversation were judged more satisfying than apologies that came at the very start. The reason seemed to be that a later apology came after the hurt person had been heard. An apology at the first moment, before they had said anything, could feel like an attempt to close the subject.

This fits a common experience. A man realises he has upset his partner or a friend, rushes in with “I'm sorry, I'm sorry,” and is met with something like “You don't even know what you're apologising for.” Often, that is true.

So listen first. Ask what happened from their side, and let them tell you without interrupting or defending. Sit down if you can. Nod to show that you have understood, as the chapter on the head nod described, even where you might tell the story differently. Reflect back what you have heard: “So when I didn't call, it felt like I didn't care.” Only then apologise, and apologise for what they have told you, not only for what you had assumed.

The figure here listens, attentive and unhurried. In an apology, this posture comes before any words of your own. It tells the other person that what they feel matters more to you than ending the conversation.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if apologies at the very start of a conversation were generally received as well as those that followed listening. Frantz and Bennigson's studies were small, so the finding should be read as a strong suggestion rather than a rule.

teach.h: The body of a real apology.
teach.p:
An apology is one of the moments that the opening chapter of this part said needs the face. Turn toward the person. Approach at a pace they can accept, and stop at a distance they are comfortable with; if they step back, stay where you are. If they are seated, sit too, rather than standing over them.

Let your body stop defending itself. Unfold your arms. Keep your hands still and visible, loosely clasped or open. Lower your head a little, or simply soften your posture, so that you are not looming. Look at them steadily, without staring, and let them look away if they need to. Slow your voice and lower it slightly. Leave pauses.

Watch for the signs of a non-apology, which people pick up at once: a shrug as you say sorry; a smirk or a laugh; arms folded or hands in pockets; the chin lifted; the body side-on, ready to leave; a glance at a phone or a clock; the word “but” arriving halfway through. “I'm sorry if you were offended” spoken with a shrug is an accusation, not an apology.

Then say the words that matter most, plainly: what you did, that it was your fault, that you regret it, and what you will do now. The figure here stands with hands clasped quietly in front, head level, still. There is nothing defensive in the posture and nothing performed. That stillness makes the words believable.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if listeners judged apologies only by their words, ignoring tone, posture and expression. Research on emotional expression and on how sincerity is judged suggests otherwise, though few studies have tested apology delivery directly.

teach.p:
Many men try to apologise with a straight face, as if any sign of discomfort would weaken them. The research suggests the opposite. In 1995 Dacher Keltner described a distinct display of embarrassment: the gaze drops, a smile appears and is held in check, the head turns down or away, and a hand often goes to the face. He argued that the display works as appeasement, a signal that a person knows they have broken a rule and does not intend to defend the breach.

People respond to it accordingly. In a 1982 study by Gün Semin and Antony Manstead, people who watched someone knock over a display in a shop liked that person more if he showed embarrassment than if he did not. In 2012 Matthew Feinberg, Robb Willer and Keltner found that people who showed embarrassment were seen as more trustworthy and more generous, and were trusted more in economic games.

So do not hide it. The reddening face, the awkward half-smile, the downward glance and the hand rubbing the back of the neck are part of what makes an apology believable. Men are often taught to suppress these signs, and their apologies sound colder for it.

The figure here looks down and away, the classic posture of embarrassment. In an apology, a moment of this, followed by looking back up and saying what you need to say, is more convincing than a steady, unbothered gaze.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people who showed embarrassment after a mistake were judged no more favourably than those who did not. Several studies have found that they are, though most used staged scenarios, and in some settings visible embarrassment may be read as weakness.

teach.p:
Two feelings can follow a wrongdoing, and they lead in opposite directions. The psychologist June Tangney and her colleagues distinguish guilt, which focuses on the act (I did a bad thing), from shame, which focuses on the self (I am a bad person). In their research, guilt tends to motivate repair: confessing, apologising, making amends. Shame tends to motivate hiding, denial and withdrawal, and sometimes anger turned outward.

The two look different in the body. Shame shrinks: the shoulders round, the head drops, the face is hidden, the person wants to disappear. Or it flips into defence: the chin lifts, the voice rises, and the man who did wrong becomes angry at the person he wronged. The chapter on anger in Part II described anger as a guard for something softer; shame is often what it is guarding. Guilt, by contrast, turns toward the other person, because it wants to put something right.

For many men, an apology fails not because they do not care but because shame takes over. The wrongdoing feels like a verdict on their whole self, and that is unbearable, so they defend. The way through is to separate the act from the self. You did something hurtful; that does not make you a bad man, and owning it is what a good one does.

The figure here is contracted, folded in on himself. This is shame. An apology made from here usually collapses into excuses or anger. Find your way to guilt, which faces outward, before you try.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if shame motivated apology and repair as readily as guilt does. Tangney's research suggests it does not, though the two feelings often occur together, and the distinction is clearer in theory than in any particular moment.
teach.pullQuote: You did something hurtful; that does not make you a bad man, and owning it is what a good one does.

teach.p:
An apology is not a transaction, and the other person does not owe you forgiveness for making one. Lewicki's study found that asking for forgiveness was the least important part of an apology; pressing for it is worse. If the other person's arms stay folded, if they say they need time, if they say thank you but nothing more, accept it. Give them room, and let the offer of repair do its work over days and weeks.

Repair is often physical and practical: turning up when you said you would, doing the job you neglected, being there next time. Between men, it often looks like the side-by-side gestures of earlier chapters: an offer of help with a move, a lift to the hospital, a pint bought without comment. These are not substitutes for saying sorry; they are what makes the saying believable.

Learn to receive apologies too, especially from men who find them hard. A man who cannot quite say sorry may offer a repair attempt instead, as the previous chapter described: an awkward joke, a cup of tea, a hand on your shoulder, a text about something else. If you are ready, meet it. If you are not, say so kindly. A man whose clumsy apology is mocked may not try again.

The figures here shake hands. Sometimes this is where an apology ends, days or weeks later. It cannot be demanded, only made possible.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if pressing for forgiveness made reconciliation more likely. Lewicki's findings, and the experience of mediators, suggest that it does not, though people differ in how quickly they are ready to forgive.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Apologising to the side of his head
poseGallery.annotation: An apology needs the face. Turn toward him, at a distance he can accept, and say it plainly.

poseGallery.doCaption: Still hands, head a little lowered
poseGallery.dontCaption: Sorry, with arms folded and chin up
poseGallery.annotation: A defended body turns sorry into a request to close the subject. Unfold, soften, slow down.
Forgiveness cannot be demanded. Make the apology, offer repair, and give him room and time.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sorry face to face, after listening
poseGallery.dontCaption: Sorry by text, from the sofa
poseGallery.annotation: A text can carry the words but not the body that makes them believable. For what matters, turn up, and turn to face them.

poseGallery.doCaption: Down at his level, saying sorry
poseGallery.dontCaption: Apologising to a child from above
poseGallery.annotation: A child hears an apology from above as a telling-off. At his level, in plain words, it teaches him how mistakes are put right.

poseGallery.doCaption: Owning the act, standing still to say it
poseGallery.annotation: Shame hides; guilt repairs. Separating what you did from who you are makes it possible to face the person and say sorry.

caseStudy:
Neil, thirty-nine, misses the funeral of his best friend Marcus's father because of a work trip he could have moved. He sends a text that morning and means to call afterwards, but the week is busy and he does not. Over the next month Marcus goes cool. His messages are short. He skips five-a-side twice. When they do meet, his greeting is a nod rather than the usual pull-in hug.

Neil thinks it is a bad patch and that Marcus will come round. It is his wife who points out that missing the funeral was not a small thing. Neil sends a text: “Sorry mate, work was mental, should've called.” Marcus replies with a thumbs-up and nothing else.

A week later Neil asks if they can meet, and they sit on a bench outside the ground before a match. Neil asks Marcus how he has been since the funeral, and then listens. Marcus says that he looked for Neil in the church, and that not seeing him felt like being told he did not matter. Neil does not interrupt or explain.

Then he turns to face him. His face is red and he looks down for a moment before he speaks. He says that he chose work over being there, that it was his fault and nobody else's, that he is sorry, and that if Marcus will let him, he would like to go with him to the grave. Marcus's arms stay folded. He says, “Right,” and they watch the match.

Ten days later Marcus texts a time and the name of the cemetery. They stand there for twenty minutes, side by side, and on the way back to the car Marcus puts his arm around Neil's shoulders for a moment.
observe: Notice the next apology you witness and how the body delivering it supports or undercuts the words.
Notice signs that someone may be owed an apology by you: a cooler greeting, shorter messages, a silence where there was talk.
Notice your own body when you realise you have done something wrong: does it shrink, defend or turn toward the person?
Notice how men around you apologise without saying sorry, through jokes, favours or practical help.

drills.name: The Six Parts
steps: Think of something you need to apologise for, large or small.
Write a sentence for each component: regret, explanation, responsibility, repentance, repair and forgiveness.
Cross out any excuse hiding in the explanation.
Rewrite the apology around responsibility and repair, keeping it short.
Read it aloud and remove anything that asks for forgiveness.
variations: Do the six parts for an apology you received once, and mark which parts it had and which it lacked.
Write the apology in a version for a text message and a version for a face-to-face conversation, and compare them.

drills.name: Listen First
steps: Before your next apology, plan the question you will ask to hear the other person's side.
Plan where you will sit so that you are at the same level.
During the conversation, let them speak without interrupting, and reflect back what you heard.
Only then apologise, for what they told you.
Afterwards, note how the order changed the conversation.
variations: Ask the other person, before you apologise, whether now is a good time, and accept their answer.
Practise asking "What was it like for you?" aloud, several times, until it comes easily and without strain.

drills.name: Defence Check
steps: Stand in front of a mirror and say “I'm sorry” in the way you usually would.
Notice your arms, hands, chin, shoulders and voice.
Say it again with your arms unfolded, hands still, head a little lowered and voice slower.
Notice how different the two feel and look.
variations: Record yourself on your phone saying sorry both ways, and watch the recordings with the sound off.
Ask someone you trust to watch you say sorry and tell you which version looked more sincere.

drills.name: Act and Self
steps: Recall a time when you defended yourself instead of apologising.
Write what you did, in one sentence about the act, not about yourself.
Write what you feared it said about you.
Write a sentence separating the two, such as “I did a thoughtless thing; I am not a thoughtless person, and I can put it right.”
variations: Write one sentence about the act and one about yourself for a mistake from your childhood, and notice the difference.
Ask a friend how they separate what they did from who they are, and note any phrase you could borrow.

quiz.q: A friend says that a proper apology must end with asking for forgiveness. What did Lewicki and colleagues find?
options: Asking for forgiveness was the most important part of any apology
Responsibility and an offer of repair mattered most; forgiveness least
Explanations mattered most, because they show the reasons for it
All six components mattered equally, so the order was unimportant
quiz.explain: Acknowledging responsibility was by far the most important component, with an offer of repair second, and asking for forgiveness was the least important. Pressing for forgiveness can make the apology about the person apologising.

quiz.q: Why did Schumann and Ross conclude that men apologise less often than women?
options: Men refuse to apologise even when they agree they caused offence
Men feel apologies threaten their status, whatever the offence
Men have a higher threshold for noticing they have caused offence
Men apologise more, but quietly, so that their apologies are missed
quiz.explain: When men and women believed they had caused offence, they apologised at similar rates. Men rated the same offences as less severe, so they noticed fewer occasions that needed an apology.

quiz.q: What did Frantz and Bennigson find about the timing of apologies?
options: Apologies after the hurt person had been heard tended to work better
Apologies were always best made in the very first sentence
Timing made no difference to how an apology was received
Apologies were only effective if they were made within the first hour
quiz.explain: Later apologies were judged more satisfying because the hurt person had been heard first. An apology at the very start could feel like an attempt to close the subject.

quiz.q: What did research by Semin and Manstead, and by Feinberg and colleagues, suggest about showing embarrassment after a mistake?
options: People who showed embarrassment were judged weaker and much less trustworthy
Embarrassment made no difference to how people were judged afterwards
Only women benefited from showing embarrassment, never men
People who showed it were liked and trusted more than those who did not
quiz.explain: People who showed embarrassment after a mishap were liked more, and were seen as more trustworthy and generous. A visible moment of discomfort makes an apology more believable.

quiz.q: You have apologised sincerely to a friend, but his arms are still folded and he says only “Right.” What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask him directly whether he forgives you, so that you both know where you stand
Repeat the apology more forcefully, so that he understands how sorry you are
Accept it, give him room, and let your offer of repair do its work over time
Point out that you have apologised properly and that it is his turn to move on
quiz.explain: Forgiveness cannot be demanded, and pressing for it makes the apology about you. Accepting his response and following through on repair gives reconciliation room to happen.

quiz.q: You snapped at a colleague in a meeting yesterday. What fits this chapter best?
options: Send a quick message saying sorry if anyone was offended by it
Meet privately, hear how it landed, then own it and say how you'll put it right
Apologise in the next meeting before she has had a chance to speak
Say nothing, since bringing it up again will only make things worse
quiz.explain: An apology that follows listening, owns the act plainly and offers repair, delivered face to face in private, matches what the research suggests works. “Sorry if anyone was offended” avoids responsibility.

quiz.q: How did Dacher Keltner describe the display of embarrassment?
options: The gaze drops, a smile is held in check, the head turns down and a hand may go to the face
The chin lifts, the eyes widen, and the person stares directly at whoever is watching
The arms fold tightly, the jaw sets, and the body turns squarely towards the other person
No consistent display, since embarrassment never shows on the face or in the body
quiz.explain: Keltner described dropping gaze, a controlled smile, the head turning down or away and often a hand to the face, and argued that the display works as appeasement. A little embarrassment helps an apology land.

quiz.q: At a family lunch, you made a joke about your sister's weight. She smiled tightly, left early and has not replied to messages since. What fits this chapter best?
options: Send a quick text saying you didn't mean anything by it, and move on
Wait for her to bring it up, since it was only a joke and she will get over it
Ask to talk, listen first, then apologise for what she tells you it did
Apologise in the family chat at once, before she has a chance to say anything
quiz.explain: The signs say an apology is owed. Asking to talk, listening first and then owning the act, without excuses, is what Frantz and Bennigson's and Lewicki's research suggests works.

quiz.q: Someone says that "Sorry if anyone was offended" is a perfectly good apology. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since it includes the word sorry and goes to everyone involved
It shifts responsibility to the hurt person; own the act and offer repair instead
It is right, but only if it is sent by email rather than said in person
It is wrong, because apologies should never mention anyone else's feelings
quiz.explain: "If anyone was offended" makes the other person's reaction the problem. Lewicki's research found acknowledging responsibility and offering repair mattered most.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific apology you owe, or one you made that did not work. Describe what you did, how the other person responded at the time, and what their body has said since. If you made an apology, how did your body deliver it: arms, voice, face, timing? Did shame push you toward defending yourself? Write the apology you would make now, built around responsibility and repair, and describe where and how you would make it.
reflection.guidance: Be specific about the act, and keep the apology about the act rather than about your character. If you notice yourself writing excuses, cross them out and see what remains. If the apology is owed to someone who may not want contact, consider whether making it serves them or only you, and respect their choice.

failureMode: The first failure is not to notice that an apology is owed, because men tend to rate offences as less serious than the people they hurt. The second is to apologise too soon, before the other person has been heard, so that the apology feels like an attempt to close the subject. The third is to let the body contradict the words: folded arms, a lifted chin, a shrug, a smirk, an eye on the clock, a “but.” The fourth is to let shame turn an apology into a defence or an attack. And the fifth is to demand forgiveness, or to give up when it does not come at once, rather than letting repair do its work over time. Listen, face him, own it, offer repair, and give him room.

moreCases.title: The apology at the door
moreCases.scene:
Dev, forty, was supposed to collect his daughter, Mia, eight, from her swimming lesson at five. He got caught up on a work call and forgot.
  The swimming teacher rang his wife, Anita, who left a meeting early and drove across town in rush-hour traffic to collect Mia, who had been waiting
  in the foyer, upset, for forty minutes.

  When Anita walks through the front door with Mia, Dev is already in the hallway. Before she has taken her coat off, he says, quickly, "I'm so
  sorry, I completely forgot, the call ran over, it won't happen again." He reaches for her bag.

  Anita does not hand it over. She says, "Right," in a flat voice, and walks past him into the kitchen. Mia goes upstairs without speaking. Dev
  stands in the hall, confused. He apologised immediately, and properly, he thinks. Why does it feel as though it made things worse?

Dev had seen the swimming teacher's missed calls on his phone at twenty to six, and felt sick. He rang Anita, who was already in the car. She said only, "I'm getting her," and hung up. He spent the next half hour rehearsing his apology.

Mia had been the last child left in the foyer. The swimming teacher had waited with her, and Mia had told her that her daddy always forgot things, which Anita heard as she walked in.

Anita had also had to explain to her manager why she was leaving a client meeting early, which she hated doing, and had spent the drive feeling that her work was always the one that gave way.
moreCases.misread:
Dev read the speed of his apology as a sign of sincerity, and assumed that apologising at once, before anything else could be said, was the best way to show he cared. He read Anita's flat "Right" as a refusal to accept it.

He also read his own discomfort as something to get rid of quickly. Much of the speed of his apology was about ending his own guilt, not about Anita's afternoon.

He also apologised to Anita and not to Mia, who had been the one waiting. The person most hurt is not always the person who arrives at the door first.

Mia's silence on the stairs was a message too, and a clearer one than Anita's "Right".
moreCases.betterRead: Frantz and Bennigson found that apologies coming later in a conversation were often judged more satisfying than apologies at the very start, because a later apology came after the hurt person had been heard. Dev's apology at the door, before Anita had said a word, took away her chance to say what the forty minutes had been like, for her and for Mia, and it sounded like an attempt to close the subject. It also included an excuse, the call, and a promise, but no acknowledgement of what she had gone through. The better approach was to let her speak first. After dinner, Dev sat down at the table with her and said, "Tell me what happened this afternoon." Anita told him about leaving her meeting, the traffic, and Mia's face in the foyer. Dev listened, without interrupting or explaining. Then he said, "I'm sorry. That was my job and I forgot it, and you both paid for it. I'll put the pickups in my calendar with an alarm." Then he went upstairs and said the same to Mia, kneeling by her bed.

moreCases.title: Sorry if anyone was offended
moreCases.scene:
Phil, fifty-two, a department head, loses his temper in a team meeting when a junior analyst, Jordan, twenty-four, points out an error in
  Phil's figures. Phil tells him, in front of eight colleagues, that he should check his own work before he starts criticising other people's. Jordan
  goes red and says nothing for the rest of the meeting.

  That evening, Phil feels uneasy. He sends an email to the whole team: "Apologies if anyone was offended by my tone in this afternoon's meeting.
  It's been a stressful week. Let's move forward."

  The next morning, two colleagues mention the email to Jordan with raised eyebrows. Jordan does not reply to it. In the team meeting that afternoon,
  he sits at the far end of the table and does not speak.

Phil's own manager, who heard about the meeting from someone else, mentioned it to him the next morning, which is partly why Phil sent the email. He wanted to be seen to have dealt with it.

Jordan's mother rang him that evening and asked how work was going. He said fine. He did not tell her that he had spent the train journey home wondering whether to start looking for another job, because the one thing he had been told when he joined was that the department valued people who spoke up.

Two of the colleagues who had laughed at Phil's remark in the meeting have since been noticeably cooler towards Jordan, taking their lead from the head of department.
moreCases.misread:
Phil read his email as an apology. It contained the word, it went to everyone, and it moved things on. Jordan read it as something else: a statement that placed the problem in other people's feelings, offered an excuse and asked for the matter to be closed.

He also read the stressful week as a reason the team should understand, when it was a reason he had behaved badly, which is not the same thing.

And by sending it to everyone, he spread the moment further while giving Jordan nothing, which made the email worse than silence.

Phil also chose the medium that let him avoid Jordan's face. An email is easier to send than an apology is to say, which is exactly why it carries less.
moreCases.betterRead:
Lewicki, Polin and Lount found that two parts of an apology mattered most: acknowledging responsibility and offering repair. "Apologies if anyone was offended" does neither. It makes the hurt person's reaction the problem, rather than the act, and "it's been a stressful week" turns the apology into an explanation. A public harm also usually needs a public correction, and an email cannot carry the body that makes an apology believable. Phil's better approach, which a colleague he trusted suggested, was to do it properly, twice. He asked Jordan for ten minutes, sat across a small table at his level, and said, "I was out of order yesterday. You were right about the figures, and I attacked you instead of thanking you. I'm sorry." Then, at the next team meeting, he said to the room that Jordan had caught an important error and that he had handled it badly. Jordan said thank you. A month later, he pointed out another error, and Phil thanked him.

Phil also told his own manager what he had done, which his manager said was the most useful part.

moreCases.title: The son who missed the seventieth
moreCases.scene:
Kofi, thirty-eight, missed his father's seventieth birthday party because he chose to go on a stag weekend that had been booked for months.
  He told himself his father would understand. His father, Kwame, has said nothing about it since, but he has been cool on the phone, and at Sunday
  lunch three weeks later, he greets Kofi with a handshake instead of the usual embrace.

  After lunch, Kofi finds his father in the garden. He stands in front of him and says that he is sorry he missed the party, that it was a stupid
  choice, and that he should have been there. His father listens with his arms folded, looks at the roses and says, "Right." Nothing else.

  Kofi feels a flash of frustration. He has done the hard thing, and his father has given him nothing back. He is tempted to say, "I said I'm sorry,
  Dad. What more do you want?"

At the party, Kwame's brother gave a speech that mentioned all four of Kwame's children by name, and then said, "three of whom are here." Kofi's mother told him about it afterwards. Kofi has not stopped thinking about it.

Kofi's sister has told him that their father was quiet for the whole party, and that he kept looking at the door. Kofi had pictured his father hardly noticing his absence among sixty guests.
moreCases.misread:
Kofi read his father's folded arms and single word as a refusal to forgive, and felt that an apology made deserved an apology accepted. He nearly turned the moment into a demand.

He also nearly forgot that the hurt was three weeks old for his father and three minutes old for him. One sentence could not be expected to undo three weeks.

He also read the handshake at the door as coldness to be overcome, rather than as information about how much the absence had hurt.

And his father's silence was, in its way, an answer. Some men can say "I'm hurt" only by saying nothing at all.
moreCases.betterRead:
An apology is not a transaction, and the other person does not owe forgiveness for receiving one. Lewicki's study found that asking for forgiveness was the least important part of an apology, and pressing for it is worse. Kwame's folded arms and his "Right" did not necessarily mean rejection. They may have meant that he had heard it and needed time, or that he was too moved to say more, or that the hurt would take more than one sentence to mend. The better response was to accept that and let repair do its work over weeks. Kofi said, "OK. I mean it, Dad," and stayed in the garden for a while, helping him tie up the roses. Over the next two months, he rang his father every Sunday and drove over twice to help with the shed. At Christmas, his father opened his arms first. He never mentioned the party again, and neither did Kofi.

Kofi also wrote his father a card for the next birthday, by hand, saying how much he had missed being there.

moreCases.title: The friend he could not face
moreCases.scene:
Matt, twenty-nine, borrows his friend Ade's car for a weekend and, reversing in a car park, crushes the rear bumper against a bollard. The
  repair will cost hundreds of pounds. Matt is mortified. He returns the car on Monday with a short message saying there is a bit of damage at the
  back and he is really sorry, and then he stops replying to Ade's messages. He skips five-a-side. He avoids the pub on Fridays. When Ade rings, he lets
  it go to voicemail.

  Ade is less angry about the bumper than about the silence. He tells a mutual friend that Matt has ghosted him over a car, and that he never thought
  Matt was that kind of person.

  Matt, meanwhile, is lying awake telling himself that he is useless, that he always ruins things, and that Ade must hate him.

Ade has also messaged twice to ask whether Matt is all right, not about the car. Matt has read both messages and not replied, because he does not know how to answer kindness when he feels he deserves anger.

Ade's partner has started asking whether Matt is coming to their barbecue next month, and Ade does not know what to say. The bumper has been fixed already, by a friend of Ade's who runs a garage, at cost. Ade has not told Matt, because Matt has not answered his calls.
moreCases.misread:
Matt read his own mistake as a verdict on himself, I am a useless person, rather than as an act he could put right. Ade read Matt's withdrawal as indifference, when it was shame.

And by treating the mistake as proof of his worthlessness, he made the apology impossible, because nobody wants to stand in front of a friend and confirm that they are useless.

Ade's reading, that Matt did not care, was also wrong, and understandable. From outside, shame and indifference can look exactly the same.

Matt's silence also left Ade to invent his own explanation, which, without information, was the least kind one.
moreCases.betterRead:
June Tangney's research distinguishes guilt, which focuses on the act, from shame, which focuses on the self. Guilt tends to motivate repair: apologising, making amends. Shame tends to motivate hiding, withdrawal and avoidance. Matt's shame turned a dented bumper into a failure of character, and the hiding it produced did far more damage to the friendship than the bumper had. The better approach starts by separating the act from the self: "I damaged Ade's car" is something that can be fixed; "I am useless" is not. Matt's brother, when Matt finally told him, made him say the first sentence aloud. Then Matt rang Ade, and said, "I'm sorry about the car, and I'm sorry I disappeared. I was embarrassed. I'll pay the repair, whatever it costs." Ade said he had been more worried than angry. Matt paid the garage bill. At five-a-side the next week, Ade put an arm round his shoulders before kick-off and said that the bumper had been ugly anyway.

Matt also noted, later, that the bumper cost three hundred pounds, and the month of silence had nearly cost him a friend.

workedReading.title: Apologising for a cruel joke
workedReading.scene:
At a family Sunday lunch, Sam, thirty-four, makes a joke about his sister Becky's weight when she takes a second helping of potatoes. A few people laugh. Becky puts her fork down, smiles tightly and says nothing. She leaves early, saying she has a headache. Over the following week, her messages to the family group chat stop, and when Sam sends her a video of a dog that he knows she would usually love, she does not reply. Sam's mother tells him, on the phone, that Becky was very upset, and that she has been trying to lose weight for months.

Sam has always been the family joker, and the jokes have often been at other people's expense. Nobody has ever complained before, at least not to him, and he realises now that this may not mean nobody minded.

Becky is his younger sister by three years. Growing up, Sam teased her constantly, and their parents always said that it was what brothers did. He realises now that she may have spent thirty years waiting for him to stop.

Sam also knows that Becky is the one who organises the family lunches, buys their mother's birthday presents and remembers everyone's anniversaries. If she stops coming, the whole family will feel it.

steps.label: Notice that it is owed
steps.text:
Sam's first instinct was that it was just a joke and that Becky was overreacting. Then he notices the signs: her tight smile and silence at the table, the early exit, the silent group chat, the unanswered video. Schumann and Ross found that men tend to rate offences as less serious than the people they hurt, and Sam realises that his sense of the joke as small is not the measure that matters.

He also notices that his first defence, "it was just a joke", is a story about him, about what he intended. The question is not what he meant but what it did to her.

He also notices that his mother had to tell him. He had seen Becky's tight smile at the table and chosen not to read it, because reading it would have meant admitting the joke had landed badly.

steps.label: Do not rush it
steps.text:
His second instinct is to send a quick message: "Sorry about the joke, didn't mean anything by it." He does not. A quick text would close the subject before Becky has said anything, and "didn't mean anything by it" is an excuse. He messages instead: "I think I upset you on Sunday. Could I come round and talk?" She replies the next day, briefly: Thursday.

He also notices how much he wants this over quickly. The urge to apologise by text is partly about sparing himself an uncomfortable conversation, and that is a reason to resist it.

He also lets her choose the time and place. Asking "Could I come round?" rather than turning up gives her control, which matters after a moment in which she had none.

steps.label: Arrange the body
steps.text:
At Becky's flat, he waits to be asked in, and sits when she sits, at the kitchen table, across a corner from her rather than directly opposite. He keeps his arms unfolded and his hands still on the table. He does not slump or sprawl. He knows that this is one of the conversations that needs the face, so he turns towards her.

He also leaves his phone in his coat, so that it cannot buzz on the table between them. A phone on the table, even face down, tells someone that they are competing for your attention.

He also notices that he wants to sit back with his arms folded, which is how he usually sits when he is uncomfortable. He keeps them on the table, which feels exposed and is meant to.

He also lets himself be the one who is less comfortable. Taking the chair with its back to the door, or the lower seat, is a small physical way of not claiming the stronger position.

steps.label: Listen first
steps.text:
He says, "I want to say sorry for Sunday, but first I want to hear what it was like for you." Becky is quiet, then says that she has been dieting for months, that she was proud of how she had been doing, and that being laughed at in front of the whole family made her feel about twelve. Sam listens without interrupting, explaining or defending. He feels his face go hot and lets it.

He also resists the urge to say that he did not know about the diet. It would be true, and it would turn her account of being hurt into an argument about whether he could have known.

He also resists the urge to nod quickly or say "I know, I know" while she speaks, which would hurry her and suggest he had already understood before she finished.

steps.label: Own it, plainly
steps.text:
When she has finished, he says, "I'm sorry. It was a cruel thing to say, and I said it in front of everyone. You didn't deserve it." He does not say that he did not mean it, or that he was only joking. His gaze drops for a moment as he says it, and he lets that happen too: a little visible embarrassment tells her that he knows he broke something.

He also keeps it short. A long apology can become a speech about the speaker's feelings, and the person who was hurt ends up comforting the person who hurt them.

He also does not add a self-criticism, such as "I'm an idiot". It would invite her to reassure him, which would turn the apology into something she had to do for him.

steps.label: Offer repair, not a demand
steps.text:
He says that he will apologise in the family chat as well, if she would like, so that everyone knows it was wrong, and that he will not make jokes about her body again. He does not ask her to forgive him. Becky says she would like him to say something in the chat. Her arms are still folded, and she says she needs a bit of time.

He also does not ask whether they are all right now, or whether she is still upset. Those questions put the burden of reassurance on her, which is exactly what an apology should not do.

He also asks whether there is anything else she would like him to do. She says no, the chat message will be enough. Asking leaves the shape of the repair in her hands.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Sam posts a short message to the family: "I was out of order on Sunday and I've apologised to Becky." Becky replies with a single heart. Over the next few weeks, she starts posting in the chat again, and at the next lunch, she sits next to him. Sam notes that the apology itself took five minutes, and that most of the work was in noticing it was owed, waiting until she could be heard, and keeping his body from defending him while he said it.

He also notices, at the next few family meals, how often he reaches for a joke at someone's expense, and how often he can choose a different one. The repair, he realises, is mostly in what he does not say.

Becky tells him, months later, that the apology mattered less than the fact that the jokes stopped. That, she says, was how she knew he had meant it.

moreFailures.title: Not noticing that an apology is owed
moreFailures.body:
Schumann and Ross found that men and women apologise at similar rates when they think they have done something wrong, but that men tend to rate offences as less serious, and so notice fewer occasions that need an apology. The result is men who are genuinely surprised to learn, weeks later, that a remark, a missed event or a forgotten promise hurt someone badly. The signs are often in the body of the person hurt: a cooler greeting, shorter messages, a missing face at the usual gathering, a tight smile. Watch for them, and when you see them, ask whether you owe something, rather than waiting to be told.

It also helps to ask, when someone you know goes cool, "Have I done something to upset you?" Many people who are waiting for an apology will not ask for one, but will answer a direct, kind question.

It also helps to remember that people often do not tell you directly. A cooler greeting, a shorter text, a missed gathering: these are often the only signals you will get, and they deserve a question.

Partners often notice that an apology is owed before the man does, as Neil's wife did in this chapter's case study. If someone close to you says "I think you should say sorry", it is worth taking seriously even if you cannot yet see why.

moreFailures.title: Apologising too soon
moreFailures.body:
It feels responsible to apologise at once, and sometimes it is. But Frantz and Bennigson found that apologies at the very start of a conversation, before the hurt person has spoken, can feel less satisfying, because they seem designed to close the subject. An apology lands best after the other person has been heard: after they have said what it was like, and you have listened without defending or explaining. Ask first, listen properly, and then apologise for what you now understand, rather than for what you assumed.

There is a balance here. Waiting too long can look like indifference, and an apology weeks later may come too late. The aim is to apologise soon after the person has been heard, not to delay for its own sake.

It also helps to ask permission to apologise, if the moment is raw. "Can I say something about yesterday?" lets the other person decide whether they are ready to hear it.

It also helps to know that some people need time before they can talk at all. If they say "Not now," ask when would be good, and then come back at that time, without pressure.

And if you realise only later that you apologised too soon, it is fine to go back: "I said sorry quickly yesterday, but I didn't really listen. Can you tell me what it was like?"

moreFailures.title: Letting the body contradict the words
moreFailures.body:
"I'm sorry" said with folded arms, a lifted chin, a shrug, a smirk, an eye on the clock or a voice that rises at the end is heard as something other than an apology. People judge sincerity largely from the body, and a defensive body cancels the words. Turn towards the person, at their level. Unfold your arms. Keep your hands still and visible. Lower your head a little. Speak slowly and quietly. Let some embarrassment show: Keltner's research suggests that a visible display of embarrassment works as appeasement, telling the other person that you know a rule was broken.

It also helps to watch your voice. An apology said quickly, in a rising tone, sounds defensive. One said slowly, in a lower, steadier voice, sounds like it was meant.

It also helps to watch your face as you finish. A smile of relief straight after an apology can look as though you are glad it is over, rather than sorry for what you did.

It also helps to put down whatever you are holding. Keys, a phone, a cup or a bag in your hands while you apologise can look as though you are on your way somewhere else.

moreFailures.title: Making a non-apology, or demanding forgiveness
moreFailures.body:
"Sorry if you were offended", "Sorry, but you have to understand", "I've said I'm sorry, what more do you want?" are not apologies. The first makes the other person's feelings the problem; the second turns the apology into an excuse; the third turns it into a demand. Lewicki's study found that acknowledging responsibility and offering repair mattered most, and that asking for forgiveness mattered least. Own the act, offer to put it right, and then accept whatever the other person gives back, including folded arms and a request for time.

It also helps to notice the "but". Anything that follows "I'm sorry, but" usually cancels the apology, because it tells the other person that what you really want to say comes next.

It also helps to resist asking "Are we OK?" straight away. It asks the other person to close the matter on your timetable, which is a quieter way of demanding forgiveness.

And beware the apology that asks for something in return, such as "I'm sorry, and I hope you'll be sorry too." However fair it feels, it turns the apology into a negotiation.

questions.a:
Lewicki, Polin and Lount identified six common parts of an apology: regret, explanation, acknowledgement of responsibility, repentance, an offer of repair and a request for forgiveness. Apologies with more of them were rated as more effective, but two mattered far more than the rest: acknowledging responsibility and offering repair. In practice, that means saying plainly what you did, without excuses, and offering something concrete to put it right. Add to that the timing, after the other person has been heard, and a body that is not defending itself, and you have most of what an apology needs.

It also helps to keep the explanation short or leave it out entirely. Explanations easily turn into excuses, and the other person usually does not need to know why you did it as much as that you know you did.

It also helps to make the repair proportionate. A forgotten pickup needs a calendar alarm; a public humiliation needs a public correction; a broken trust needs months of reliable behaviour.

It also helps to say it in your own words. A formula learned from a book can sound rehearsed; plain words, said slowly, sound meant.

questions.q: Why do so many men find it hard to apologise?
questions.a:
Partly because of what Schumann and Ross found: men tend to set a higher threshold for what counts as an offence, so they notice fewer occasions that call for an apology. Partly because many men were taught that apologising is weakness or a loss of status. And partly because of shame: when a mistake feels like a verdict on who you are, rather than something you did, it is far harder to own. Separating the act from the self, "I did a thoughtless thing" rather than "I am a thoughtless person", often makes it easier to say sorry and mean it.

It also helps to practise on small things. Men who apologise readily for small mistakes, such as being late or interrupting, often find it easier to apologise for large ones.

It also helps to watch the men around you. Many men apologise without saying sorry, through jokes, favours or turning up with a pint. These count for something, but they often leave the hurt person unsure whether the act was acknowledged.

It also helps to know that apologising does not mean losing. People generally respect someone who can admit a mistake far more than someone who never does.

It also helps to remember that apologising well is a skill, learned by practice. Few men were taught it, and almost any man can get better at it.

questions.q: Should I apologise if I do not think I did anything wrong?
questions.a:
Do not fake it: an apology you do not mean is usually visible in the body, and it can make things worse. But it is worth asking whether you might be measuring the offence by your own threshold rather than by its effect on the other person. You can also acknowledge impact honestly without claiming a fault you do not feel: "I can see that what I said really hurt you, and I'm sorry it did." That is different from "Sorry if you were offended", because it accepts that the hurt was real and caused by you. Often, listening first changes your view of what you did.

It also helps to remember that an apology can be the start of a conversation, not the end of one. Listening to why it mattered to them may change your view of whether you were wrong.

It also helps to separate the intent from the effect in your own mind. You can believe you meant no harm and still accept that harm was done. Both can be true, and an apology addresses the second.

And if, after listening, you still believe you did nothing wrong, it is honest to say so kindly, while acknowledging that they were hurt. That is better than a hollow apology that both of you will notice.

questions.q: What is wrong with "sorry if you were offended"?
questions.a:
It places the problem in the other person's reaction rather than in what you did. "If you were offended" suggests that their offence is uncertain, perhaps unreasonable, and that your apology depends on it. It also usually comes without acknowledgement of responsibility or any offer of repair, the two parts Lewicki's research found mattered most. A real apology names the act: "I'm sorry I spoke to you like that in front of everyone." If you find yourself reaching for "if", ask whether you are trying to apologise or trying to close the subject.

It also helps to notice the passive voice. "Mistakes were made" is another way of not owning the act, and people hear it for what it is.

It also helps to notice the urge to add context. Context can matter, but it can come later, after the apology has landed, if the other person asks for it.

It also helps to watch for "I'm sorry you feel that way", which does the same thing as "if", and is heard the same way.

questions.q: What if they will not forgive me?
questions.a:
Then accept it, at least for now. An apology is not a transaction, and the other person does not owe you forgiveness for making one. Folded arms, a short reply or a request for time may mean that they have heard you and need longer, or that the hurt is deeper than one apology can mend. Do not press, repeat the apology to force a response, or complain that you have done your part. Let the offer of repair do its work over days and weeks: turning up, doing what you said you would, changing the behaviour that caused the hurt. Forgiveness, if it comes, often follows the repair rather than the words.

It also helps to remember that some hurts are slow to heal, especially after a betrayal. Patience, steady behaviour and time are often the only things that rebuild trust, and they cannot be hurried.

It also helps to keep the relationship going in ordinary ways while you wait: a normal message, an invitation, a favour. These show that your apology was not a bargain, and that you will still be there either way.

It also helps to forgive yourself in the meantime. Carrying shame while you wait for someone else's forgiveness can push you back towards hiding, which helps nobody.

questions.q: How should I apologise to a child?
questions.a:
Simply, at their level and without making them responsible for your feelings. Kneel or sit so that your face is level with theirs. Say what you did, in plain words: "I'm sorry I shouted at you. That wasn't fair." Do not add a lecture about what they did to provoke it, and do not ask them to say it is all right. Offer repair if there is one, such as a promise to try a calmer way next time, and then keep it. Apologising to children teaches them that adults make mistakes and put them right, which is one of the most useful things a parent can model.

It also helps to apologise to children for small things as well as large ones. A father who says "Sorry I was grumpy this morning" shows his children that apology is ordinary, not a rare event reserved for disasters.

It also helps to apologise to a child soon. Children often carry a telling-off for longer than adults realise, and a quick, simple apology the same day can stop it settling into a story about themselves.

It also helps to say sorry to teenagers, too, even when they shrug. A shrug from a fifteen-year-old does not mean the apology did not land; it often means it did, and they do not know what to do with it.

watch.title: Rosa Apologising
watch.notice: A comic compilation of a tough detective trying to apologise. Notice how hard the body finds it, the averted eyes, the stiff posture, the words forced out, and how much a sincere apology depends on the body as well as the words.

reviewPrompt: This week, notice one apology you owe, listen before you make it, and deliver it face to face with unfolded arms and a plain statement of responsibility.
